extracted.intended_audience: travelers, readers, and students of art and architectural history (particularly Venetian/Gothic/Renaissance sepulchral monuments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for judging and composing tombs and sepulchral monuments (especially Gothic and Renaissance examples in Venice), including form, ornament, symbolism, and moral/aesthetic purpose. Intended to help a traveller or student understand what makes a tomb dignified, religiously expressive, or otherwise successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid colossal pomp for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture which appealed to the lowest instincts by seeking admirableness chiefly from being huge — built with little idea of any other admirableness than that which was to result from its being huge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'Titanic insanity' produces inanimate gigantism: buildings and churches whose religious impression depends largely on their size (e.g., large piers, colossal masses) rather than meaningful detail or spiritual content. This is presented as an aesthetic and moral failing to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance ornamentation detail and architectural mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sacrifice meaningful workmanship and delicate detail for the sake of bringing larger stones or creating monumental bulk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renaissance builders often spared detailed work to concentrate on mass and order (rustication and five orders) — the text argues for keeping a proper balance so that scale does not replace the value of careful, meaningful detail (niches, casements, doorways).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and solemnity in tomb adornment
rubrics_metrics.description: Early tombs are commended as 'simple and lovely in adornment, severe and solemn in their expression,' confessing the power and accepting the peace of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good tombs express acceptance of death and hope in Christ's righteousness; inscriptions and symbols should be modest and devotional (e.g., 'I will lay me down in peace...'). Simplicity and seriousness are virtues in sepulchral design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prideful display and terrorizing motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Later tombs that combine mean pride and miserable terror (statues of Virtues used to disguise sarcophagi, elaborate false epitaphs, portrait statues with strained animation; skulls and scythed skeletons hidden in niches) are criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such combinations — ostentatious vanity plus grotesque memento-mori devices — are presented as an unhealthy, dishonorable approach to commemorating the dead and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect Gothic tomb type (formal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal Christian/Gothic tomb consists of a raised and perfectly visible stone sarcophagus bearing a recumbent figure, the whole covered by a canopy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'perfect type' develops historically: simple sarcophagus → elaboration with figure-sculpture → canopy (four-square or arch) → life-size recumbent figure and surmounting statues. The canopy and arrangement have symbolic and compositional roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use religious bas-reliefs and central enthroned figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcophagi are often divided into panels filled with small bas-reliefs of the acts or martyrdom of patron saints, with, in the centre, Christ or the Virgin and Child enthroned under a curtained canopy; the Annunciation figures are usually at the angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such organization ties the monument to definite religious purpose: narrative panels and central sacred figures reinforce the promise of eternal life and the tomb's devotional meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration should have religious meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Tomb ornamentation ought to carry religious significance rather than be ornamental architectural frippery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italian sarcophagi are praised for being massive, smooth, and gloomy while bearing simple crosses 'dimly graven' — contrasted with English tombs that add quatrefoils, small shafts, and arches that make them merely decorative and destroy seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain conspicuousness; prioritize dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: A monument should not be conspicuous or intrusive; its primary aim is to direct thoughts toward the recumbent image and the expression of hope of resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-composed tombs 'serve only to decorate the portal' and present the history of the dead subdued into dim ornament; the remembrance of the person's dignity is achieved without ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited concession to pride for honor and affection
rubrics_metrics.description: As much concession as may consist with honor, discretion, or dignity may be granted to human pride — to record and commemorate heroic life — but no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tomb may show a dignified image of the deceased's armed youth or achievements, but these representations should be modestly integrated so as not to overwhelm the funerary and religious purpose; excess leads to erring ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of virtue-figures should be restrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing personified Virtues on a sarcophagus can signal a claim to virtues and, when excessive, shows erring ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show increasing numbers of virtue-statues correlate with declining moral modesty; inclusion of a single virtue may be tolerable, but multiple virtues crowning a tomb can be a sign of pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design sculptures for intended viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptural execution often appears 'rudely chiselled' up close yet yields tender and masterly lines when seen from the intended distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carving should consider the spectator's vantage: simplification in close detail can be appropriate if the overall lines and composition read correctly from the anticipated viewing position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use color and gilding sympathetically
rubrics_metrics.description: Tombs and their figures were historically richly colored and adorned (e.g., gilded hair, silvered wings, arabesques on garments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polychromy and metalwork contribute to the intended visual and devotional effect and should be applied thoughtfully to support the monument's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ emblematic narrative scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels representing scriptural or hagiographic scenes (Death of the Virgin, Epiphany, acts of saints) effectively occupy sarcophagus surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative sculpture provides theological framing and status-appropriate commemoration; their placement and subject should relate clearly to the tomb's devotional message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of curtains/tabernacle motif in canopy (Pisan idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pisan motif of angels withdrawing curtains to reveal a tabernacle-like setting for the enthroned sacred figure (or for looking down upon the dead) is a compositional device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curtains and tabernacle effects create perspective and layers of sacred space; they can suggest divine abstraction and the hierarchy of spiritual magnitudes (God, Angel, Man) when used with appropriate restraint and perspective.
